episode_thesis: Nick Baltas, reviewing two practitioner papers, argues that trend following earns its keep from timing (volatility clustering and medium-horizon skew), so the equity sleeve should be left unconstrained: Quantica's tests show capping equity beta gains about 50bp in the worst quarters but costs about 200bp a year in the long run, though he accepts that loss-averse investors may rationally pay that premium. He also argues that carry (especially cross-sectional or beta-neutralised, and commodity carry) is a useful complement to trend, provided its hidden spot/trend contribution is understood. Host Alan Dunne mostly probes, adding the 2017 stacked-equity worry, the 2x-drawdown rule of thumb and the skew difference between commodity and FX carry.

speakers.name: Nick Baltas
speakers.role: systematic macro quant researcher (trend, carry, reversion); main guest
speakers.speaker_note: Speaker labels are inferred from turn structure; the first-person 'we' refers to his research group and clients. Dunne's questions and Baltas's answers are cleanly separable in the captions except for a few overlapping turns in chunk C07 and C11.

worldview_premises.premise: Trend following is not only a bad-times hedge. It earns good returns in rising markets by capturing equities, so it should be judged by what it earns across regimes and not by crisis payoffs alone.
worldview_premises.support: 2024 year-to-date contribution of equities to trend programs; Quantica quarterly regime table

worldview_premises.premise: Market timing only has meaning with a horizon. Over one day it is a coin toss, but over 1-6 months volatility clustering and serial correlation make direction partly predictable, and positive skew of trend returns is evidence of that timing skill.
worldview_premises.support: an academic paper showing trend can work without return serial correlation if volatility clusters; observed positive medium-term skew

worldview_premises.premise: Time-series momentum differs from cross-sectional momentum only by a time-varying net long investment, so trend is partly a directional (beta) bet while cross-sectional strategies are market neutral.
worldview_premises.support: Goyal and Jegadeesh paper (recalled from memory)

worldview_premises.premise: Diversification pays most at turning points, and a broad, less correlated universe (for example producer/consumer-driven commodities) adds more than extra speculative markets, while macro markets are where crisis alpha comes from.
worldview_premises.support: square-root-of-N logic and the substitution effect when volatility is held constant; no data shown

worldview_premises.premise: Investors are asymmetric to gains and losses, so paying a long-term premium for downside protection can be rational even when the paper shows it is costly; the asymmetry in the Quantica result mirrors the asymmetry in risk aversion.
worldview_premises.support: loss-aversion argument; no estimate of the utility trade-off

worldview_premises.premise: Carry is the return from holding an asset if the price stays unchanged. No-arbitrage would make price changes offset it, but covered interest parity fails, so carry persists as compensation for risks such as crash risk or short supply.
worldview_premises.support: house/mortgage illustration; reference to parity failures

worldview_premises.premise: There is no universal safe volatility level or number of markets. The right risk depends on the investor's risk aversion and, for asset owners, on the nominal return target their liabilities impose.
worldview_premises.support: Markowitz frontier argument; target-date fund glide path

mechanism_chains.topic: Why capping equity exposure helps little in crises but costs a lot in bull markets (Quantica paper)

steps.from: Trend follower is net short equities in downturns (negative beta) and also earns from bonds, commodities and other classes
steps.to: CTAs are positive in 12 of the worst 16 S&P quarters since 2000: crisis beta plus crisis alpha
steps.why: timing of equity direction plus multi-asset diversification

steps.from: Remove equities or cap the long side or neutralise beta with short S&P futures
steps.to: Downside improves only slightly (about 4.1% to 4.5-4.6% in the worst quarters; no-equities variant worse at 3.7%)
steps.why: the negative beta to equities is part of the crisis payoff, but the short-only and capped variants avoid being long into a turning point

steps.from: The same constraints reduce participation in rising equity markets
steps.to: Long-run return falls from about 5.9% to about 4%: roughly 50bp gained downside for about 200bp lost long term
steps.why: equities are the largest contributor in bull regimes, and beta neutralisation shorts rising markets

steps.from: Beta constraints applied to the full portfolio
steps.to: Positions flip direction or the book loads more on negatively correlated bond longs, raising exposure to a joint equity and bond selloff such as an inflation spike
steps.why: the optimiser meets a beta cap by shorting appreciating markets or increasing bond longs

mechanism_chains.evidence: Quantica quarterly regime split (about 97 quarters, worst 16% below minus one sigma); the speaker says his own research reaches similar results.
mechanism_chains.fails_when: A quarterly regression assumes constant beta within the quarter, so the beta/alpha split is only descriptive. The paper does not say whether freed risk was redeployed or levered up, so part of the lower long-run return is just lower risk.

mechanism_chains.topic: Why trend and reversion complement each other in choppy months

steps.from: Markets reverse (June 2024: fixed income, grains, metals)
steps.to: Trend underperforms; reversals explain more than half of the month's shortfall
steps.why: trend positions are on the wrong side after the turn

steps.from: A reversion signal built on exaggerated positive skew and run cross-sectionally
steps.to: Reversion gains about 1-1.5% in the same month, mostly in commodities
steps.why: an exacerbated trend with very positive skew flags a sell; cross-section taps a different principal component than time-series trend

mechanism_chains.fails_when: Not stated; the link between skew and reversion is described as not one-to-one.

mechanism_chains.topic: Why volatility targeting limits whipsaw and cocoa-type losses

steps.to: Trend program has already cut its exposure

steps.from: Another large move against the position
steps.to: Cocoa is only the fifth-worst commodity contributor, costing about 20-30bp in a 15%-vol program
steps.why: smaller position when the move arrives

mechanism_chains.topic: Carry in trend portfolios: where the carry return really comes from

steps.from: Time-series carry goes long positive-carry assets, for example bonds on upward-sloping curves
steps.to: Portfolio picks up beta (67% correlation of time-series bond carry to bond beta)
steps.why: curves are mostly upward sloping, so almost every bond is long

steps.from: Oil in contango while price falls
steps.to: Carry portfolio is short and profits from the spot move, which is a trend payoff
steps.why: carry signal and price trend coincide

steps.from: Neutralise beta to equities and Treasuries in the optimiser
steps.to: Portfolio turns into a mix of cross-sectional and time-series carry and can short assets with positive signals

mechanism_chains.evidence: Resolve paper results as he reads them, plus his own 2017 research; the Sharpe ratio near one belongs to the optimised time-series carry portfolios.
mechanism_chains.fails_when: Cross-sectional carry weakened over five to seven years in the small Resolve universe (about 24 markets), and rolling correlations to equities and bonds drift even after being zero on average.

decision_process.practice: Choose markets for diversification and trading cost, not for past performance contribution. A sensible universe is about 50-100 markets; 10 is on the cautious side. Backtests of 40-150 markets look similar if volatility is held constant.
decision_process.why: selecting on performance is data mining (cocoa was the worst contributor until it was not); dropping markets grosses up the rest

decision_process.practice: Trend speeds from about 3 to 12 months; faster speeds lower correlation to a 60/40 portfolio because they can flip at turning points, slow speeds look net long.
decision_process.why: balance reactivity against false positives and cost; he calls this heuristics and experience, not a derived optimum

decision_process.practice: Run trend unconstrained on equities and add reversion and carry as complements; if equity beta must be limited, estimate each market's beta and cap the position-weighted sum rather than short S&P futures.
decision_process.why: unconstrained keeps timing skill and bull participation; cap by market betas captures equity beta carried by bonds and commodities

decision_process.practice: 10-15% volatility for trend alone; about 20% alongside a strategic allocation (matching equity volatility); mandates range 5-15%. For the whole portfolio, matching equity volatility (about 15%) is as aggressive as he would go. He checks that historical drawdowns stay below roughly twice volatility though he dislikes drawdown as a measure.
decision_process.why: a 5% trend sleeve does little next to a 60/40; leverage then brings financing constraints; limit reflects his personal risk aversion

decision_process.practice: Carry: bonds from curve slope and roll-down, commodities from neighbouring contracts (seasonality adjusted), currencies from the forward basis, equities from the futures-implied dividend. Standardise with a carry z-score against 1-5 years of own history; run cross-sectionally within asset class; design carry to minimise spot contribution when run alongside trend.
decision_process.why: keeps carry relative to normal, reduces beta and principal-component exposure, and avoids paying twice for trend

decision_process.practice: Add option hedges when implied volatility is cheap, even if the environment is not anti-trend.
decision_process.why: VIX near historical lows and rate volatility moderating make optionality cheap

speakers.evidence_style: Reads and interprets published practitioner and academic papers, anchors on his own research group's backtests and monthly attribution, and uses simple illustrations (mortgage example). He flags gut feelings, heuristics and subjectivity explicitly.

current_views.view: The environment (June 2024) is not anti-trend: equities strongly trending, VIX near lows, rate vol moderating. A temporary carry loss came from the Mexican peso after elections, part later recovered.
current_views.reasoning: strong equity trend and benign volatility help programs that hold equity exposure

current_views.view: Equities are by far the largest contributor to trend programs in 2024 and the rolling beta of the SG Trend index to equities is about 0.4, near a multi-year high; without equities trend would be about flat.
current_views.reasoning: dispersion between equity-constrained and unconstrained programs is the widest in years

current_views.view: Options are cheap, so adding hedges is attractive.

speakers.name: Alan Dunne
speakers.role: host sitting in for Niels Kaastrup-Larsen; CTA industry observer
speakers.speaker_note: Mostly asks questions; the views below are those he states himself or adds as context.

worldview_premises.premise: Allocating to CTAs is a systematic way to manage net equity exposure, giving crisis beta from timing and crisis alpha from multi-asset diversification; the market-timing message matters now.

Investors who hold trend on top of their own equities can be exposed to stacked long-equity risk, which is why equity limits are requested; the debate began with 2017 when trend programs were up to about 50% long equities.

Drawdown of roughly twice volatility is a rule of thumb for expected worst loss, and leverage beyond equity-like volatility is too aggressive; a 2x leveraged equity ETF would have been wiped out in 1929-32.
worldview_premises.support: historical equity fall of about 89% in 1929-32; rule of thumb

worldview_premises.premise: Non-trend strategies added to trend often are negatively skewed (like FX carry) and blunt trend convexity, but commodity carry is not, which makes it a better complement.
worldview_premises.support: performance characteristics highlighted in the Resolve paper

decision_process.practice: Frame the equity-cap question around investors' monthly P&L sensitivity, not the quarterly horizon used in the paper.
decision_process.why: investors with sensitive utility functions may accept a 2% long-run cost

decision_process.practice: Prefer commodity carry as the carry complement to trend.
decision_process.why: it is not negatively skewed, so it does not blunt trend convexity as FX carry does

speakers.evidence_style: Reports index performance figures and historical episodes (1929-32, 2017) and asks the guest to test them.

current_views.view: Trend indices turned choppy in late May to June 2024 after a strong start: Trend index -2.84% in June and +8.5% YTD, CTA index -2.2% and +7.09% YTD, with reversals in fixed income, grains and metals.

disagreements.topic: Whether capping equity exposure is worth its cost

positions.speaker: Quantica paper (reported by Baltas)
positions.position: Capping helps in downturns but the long-run price is higher, so run trend unconstrained.

positions.speaker: Nick Baltas
positions.position: Agrees with the results but argues loss-averse investors may still rationally pay a long-term premium to protect capital; the asymmetry in the result mirrors the asymmetry in risk aversion.

positions.speaker: Alan Dunne
positions.position: Agrees the cost is high but sees how it may still make sense for investors sensitive to monthly P&L (2017 stacking worry).

positions.speaker: Nick Baltas
positions.position: 10-15% for trend alone, about 20% alongside a strategic allocation; a whole portfolio at equity-matching volatility (about 15%) is as aggressive as he would go, a subjective view.

positions.speaker: Alan Dunne
positions.position: Draws on a 2x-volatility drawdown rule of thumb and the 1929-32 crash to argue leveraged equity exposure beyond equity-like volatility is too aggressive.

gaps_and_conflicts.issue: Baltas gives no statistical rule for a safe volatility level and says drawdown is a poor measure while still using the twice-volatility check; the drawdown rule of thumb assumes IID returns, which he says trend returns do not satisfy.

The cost figures for capping equities (about 50bp gained vs about 200bp lost, 100-140bp in bull quarters) are read from the captions and some numbers are garbled; the freed risk may not have been redeployed or levered, so lower risk explains part of the cost.
Crisis beta/alpha split relies on a quarterly regression with constant beta, which a trend program does not have.
Optimal trend speed range, universe size and the claim that capping may help geometric return are stated as gut feeling or heuristics with no evidence.
Resolve carry results come from a small universe (about 24 markets), so the weakening of cross-sectional carry may reflect universe size.

forward_looking_inputs: (reader) Baltas names few price-leading inputs: trend signals over 3-12 months, carry z-scores versus 1-5 year own history, a skewness-based reversion signal, implied volatility level (cheap options when VIX is low), and rolling equity beta of trend indices (about 0.4 now). Horizon for timing skill is 1-6 months, justified by volatility clustering; carry returns are described over holding periods of about a year with price risk as the offset.
reader_inferences: (reader) Baltas treats equity participation as a feature of trend, so a regime with persistent rising equities (2024) raises trend returns and equity beta together; he does not say what a prolonged equity bear market following a high beta would do beyond the paper's crisis-quarter table.

(reader) His objection to beta constraints is design-based (positions flip, bond longs increase) rather than statistical; the weak point he identifies is joint equity and bond selloffs, which links his view to inflation-shock regimes.
(reader) The carry advice reduces to a single principle: pay for carry only to the extent it is not already paid for by trend, which suggests carry should be measured net of spot movement.
